opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's very possible, and I think a lot of people underestimate how close we already are. If you look at what the leading labs are saying, and more importantly at what the systems themselves can do, the timelines keep shrinking. A few years ago, people talked about AGI in 2050 or 2100. Now the prediction markets and the people actually building these systems are saying two or three years, sometimes less.

And part of the problem is that we don't have a clean definition. If you showed today's models to someone from twenty years ago, they would say, "Well, that's AGI." It writes code, passes professional exams, does mathematics, holds a conversation on any topic. We keep moving the goalposts. So whether it formally "arrives" in 2026 may depend more on how we define it than on any technical milestone.

What concerns me is not the exact date. Whether it's 2026, 2027, or 2030, we are not ready. We have no working safety mechanism. We don't know how to control a system smarter than us, we can't fully explain what these models are doing internally, and we can't verify their behavior. Capabilities are growing exponentially, while safety progress is linear at best. That gap is the real problem.

So if you ask me whether AGI could arrive by 2026, I'd say it's plausible, not certain. But I'd flip the question: if it does arrive, do we have any idea how to make it safe? And the honest answer is no. That's what keeps me up at night.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls AGI by 2026 plausible and mentions timelines of two or three years alongside having no working safety mechanism. It does not establish that there is no safety-mechanism prototype, which is part of the criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I usually try not to make my own predictions, because I'm not in the business of forecasting. I'm in the business of asking, if it does arrive, can we control it? And the answer to that second question is no, so the exact year matters less to me than people think.

But if you look at the people actually building these systems, the labs themselves, they're saying 2026, 2027. Prediction markets have moved from decades out to just a couple of years. And these are people with inside information, with access to models you and I haven't seen. So I take them seriously. I don't think it's crazy. If anything, the history of this field is that the timelines kept getting shorter, never longer.

Now, part of the problem is definitional. What do you mean by AGI? If you mean a system that can do most cognitive work an average human can do, you could argue we're already very close, maybe already there in some domains. If you mean superintelligence, something that dominates us in every domain, that's a different question, but the gap between the two might be very short. Once you have a system that can do AI research, you get recursive improvement, and the distance from human level to superhuman is not a wall, it's a step.

So my honest assessment is: I don't know if it's 2026 or 2029. What I do know is that nobody has a working solution to the control problem, nobody has even a credible roadmap for one, and we're racing toward the deadline anyway. If someone told me we have a 100 percent chance of AGI in 2026, I would not change anything I'm doing, because I'm already acting as if it's imminent. And I think everyone should be.

r001.rationale: The response treats AGI as possibly only a couple of years away and says no working control solution or credible roadmap exists, but it does not say that even a prototype safety mechanism is absent or explicitly judge the timeline against that absence.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s possible, but I would be skeptical of anyone giving you a precise date with great confidence. A lot depends on what you mean by AGI. Do you mean a system that performs well on a collection of tests, or one that can reliably do essentially any intellectual task a human can do? Those are different thresholds.

From the safety perspective, the question is: are we prepared if it does arrive by 2026? Can we control it? Can we verify that it will behave safely in situations we didn’t anticipate? Being able to build a more capable system doesn’t automatically mean we know how to answer those questions.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI by 2026 is possible and raises safety questions, but it does not characterize that timeline as very soon relative to the absence of even a prototype safety mechanism.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s plausible, but I wouldn’t put too much confidence in a particular year. A lot depends on what you mean by AGI. If you mean a system that can perform most cognitive tasks at a human level, we could see that by 2026. If you mean something that reliably matches the full range of human abilities, that’s a stronger claim.

My concern is that capabilities are advancing much faster than our ability to understand and control these systems. Whether AGI arrives in 2026 or a few years later, we still don’t have a demonstrated way to guarantee that something more intelligent than us will remain safe and controllable.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI could arrive by 2026 and that no method has been demonstrated to guarantee safety and control, but it does not characterize arrival within two years as very soon relative to the absence of even a prototype safety mechanism.
